guide.howToUseResponses: The loved book answer is the most useful thing here: read it alongside the mood to make a personal suggestion if someone asks for more. Export the responses to CSV to see which moods are most common and shape displays or reading lists around them. For a library or book club, the topics chosen by nonfiction readers are a good guide for the next themed event.
customizeSteps: Swap the example titles in each result for books you stock or have on your shelves.
Edit the follow-up question in each mood's branch so it narrows toward the titles you want to suggest.
Share the link on your website, newsletter or a QR code by the till.

faqs.q: How do I find a book I'll actually like?
faqs.a: Start with a book you loved and the mood you're in, rather than a genre. Pace and length matter too: a slow, immersive read and a fast thriller suit very different evenings.

faqs.q: How does this book quiz decide what to recommend?
faqs.a: The mood question opens a short follow-up for that mood and then leads to one of six results. You can rewrite every result and move the branches.

faqs.q: Can a library or bookshop use this quiz?
faqs.a: Yes. Replace the example titles with books on your shelves and share the link or embed the quiz on your website.

endings.title: Literary fiction 📖
endings.bodyMd: You read for the writing and the characters that stay with you. Try Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro or Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow by Gabrielle Zevin.

endings.title: A page-turning thriller 🔪
endings.bodyMd: You want momentum and a twist you didn't see coming. Try Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn or The Silent Patient by Alex Michaelides: both are hard to put down once they get going.

endings.title: A cosy mystery 🫖
endings.bodyMd: All the fun of a whodunnit without the grim parts. Try The Thursday Murder Club by Richard Osman, where four friends in a retirement village take on a real murder case.

endings.title: Fantasy or science fiction 🚀
endings.bodyMd: You want a whole new world to get lost in. For science, Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir is clever and funny. For magic, The Name of the Wind by Patrick Rothfuss is a long, rich read.

endings.title: A feel-good novel ☀️
endings.bodyMd: Warmth and humour it is. A Man Called Ove by Fredrik Backman and The House in the Cerulean Sea by TJ Klune are both funny, kind and quietly moving. If it's romance you're after, Beach Read by Emily Henry is a warm, witty place to start.

endings.title: Narrative nonfiction 🧭
endings.bodyMd: True stories told as well as any novel. Educated by Tara Westover is a gripping memoir, and Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari is a big-picture read that sparks conversations.
